chunks: Switching frequency vs efficiency and ripple. The question: How does switching frequency impact efficiency/ripple?
Switching frequency is how many times per second the converter's switches complete a cycle. Raising it makes the ripple smaller and lets you use smaller inductors and capacitors.
But each switching event wastes a little energy, so more events means more heat. This is a trade between size and efficiency.
Imagine moving water from a well to a tank with a bucket. Many quick trips with a small bucket keep the tank level steady, so the tank can be small.
But each trip costs you a fixed bit of effort for walking, so more trips means more total effort. Fewer, bigger trips save effort but need a bigger tank to absorb the sloshing.
The analogy breaks down in that real efficiency can briefly improve with frequency, as the page explains.
With a fixed 4.
7 microhenries inductor the efficiency has a broad maximum (about 94% near 275 kilohertz): at low f the ripple current is huge and conduction and core loss rise; at high f switching loss takes over.
When the inductor is scaled to keep the ripple fixed, only the switching-loss slope remains, so efficiency falls monotonically.
Real designs lie between the curves, since larger inductors have more DCR.
Switching frequency ( f ): switching cycles per second. Ripple: the small repeating variation left on the output voltage.
Switching loss: energy wasted each time a switch changes state; total grows with f . Efficiency: output power over input power ("Why buck beats LDO efficiency").
Minimum on-time: the shortest pulse the controller can reliably make, which limits how high f can go.
Suppose each switching cycle wastes 1 µJ. At 100 kilohertz that is 1 micro J times 100 k equals 0. 1 watts. At 1 megahertz it is 1 watts, ten times more heat.
In return, with the same inductor, the ripple current is ten times smaller at 1 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"Higher switching frequency lowers ripple and shrinks L and C : inductor ripple current goes as 1 over f and the capacitor ripple as 1 over f squared .
But overlap, C oss , gate-drive, dead-time and recovery losses all scale with f , so efficiency drops.
With a fixed inductor, efficiency peaks at a moderate frequency (about 300 kilohertz in my example) because lower ripple current also cuts RMS and core loss.
With the inductor scaled to hold ripple, efficiency falls steadily. So frequency trades size against efficiency, bounded by EMI and minimum on-time."
